hints: Focus on what makes a good fire retardant here, the most smothering $\text{CO}_2$ released per gram of mineral.
Work out the $M_r$ of each mineral and remember how many $\text{CO}_2$ molecules each formula can release, 2 for barytocite and dolomite, 4 for huntite.
Compare the mass percentage of $\text{CO}_2$ for each, the highest percentage means best and the lowest means worst.
walkthrough:
**Understand what best means**

The best retardant gives the most $\text{CO}_2$ per unit mass. So we need to compare mass of $\text{CO}_2$ released divided by $M_r$ of the mineral.

General idea:
$$\text{effectiveness} = \frac{\text{mass of CO}_2 \text{ released}}{M_r \text{ of mineral}}$$

**Compare percentage of CO2 released**

Each $\text{CO}_3$ gives one $\text{CO}_2$ on heating.

Barytocite releases $2 \times 44.0 = 88.0$ g per mole:
$$\frac{88.0}{297.4} \times 100 \approx 29.6\%$$
Dolomite releases $2 \times 44.0 = 88.0$ g per mole:
$$\frac{88.0}{184.4} \times 100 \approx 47.7\%$$
Huntite releases $4 \times 44.0$ = 176.0 g per mole:
$$\frac{176.0}{353.0} \times 100 \approx 49.9\%$$
So from best to worst: huntite, then dolomite, then barytocite.

options.A: Incorrect. This puts dolomite best and huntite worst. Huntite actually releases 4 moles of CO2 per mole and has a high CO2 percentage, so it is the best, not the worst.
options.B: Incorrect. This correctly puts barytocite worst but swaps the top two. Huntite gives a slightly higher % CO2 by mass than dolomite (about 49.9% vs 47.7%), so huntite beats dolomite.
options.C: Incorrect. This correctly puts huntite best but puts barytocite before dolomite. Barytocite contains heavy Ba so its Mr is very large and its % CO2 is only about 29.6%, making it the worst.
options.D: Correct. Huntite gives the most CO2 per gram (4 CO2 from Mr 353.0, about 49.9%), dolomite is next (2 CO2 from Mr 184.4, about 47.7%), and barytocite is last because heavy Ba lowers its yield (2 CO2 from Mr 297.4, about 29.6%).
